22.t: Birth, family and first hearing music in New Orleans
22.s: La Rocca names his parents and siblings, his shoemaker father who played trumpet, riverfront and park music, and how at nine he took a cornet and taught himself tunes.
22.q: Now just tell the people who you are. This is the voice of Dominic James LaRocca, better known as Nick LaRocca, leader and manager of the world's first jazz band, known as the creators of jazz. I'll tell you about my early life in music and contact. I was born in 1889 in the city of New Orleans. My…

22.t: Father's attitude to music and the family's zither playing
22.s: La Rocca says his father pushing him might have made him quit; his siblings played by notes, including zithers and tunes like La Paloma.
22.q: C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T. Well, I'll tell you what contributed more to my musical career because my daddy did want me to play and I want to play. C-H-E-R-O-N-E-T.

259.t: His father's flute and violin playing
259.s: His father played flute and violin by ear; a story about his father recognizing a new piece shows the repertoire was old; no blues.
259.ch: Baton Rouge, Hill City and family music
259.q: I can. You say, what instruments did they play? The Piper, one we played, I played with Klein, one trampone and one guitar. They don't play no more neither. They even, they were dating to my cousin, you know, two miles, you know. Victor and them. Here they come here.

864.t: Family, cousin Joe Baptiste, and uptown Carrollton
864.s: No musicians in his family except a banjo-playing cousin, Joe Baptiste; they talk about Carrollton and the horse and mule cars.
864.q: Oh, yeah. He's older than me. Did he play with any bands? Do you remember? Yeah, he was playing with different bands, but by me being so small, I mean I wouldn't know the names of the bands. Yeah.

601.t: Uncle Amos Martin, bass horn player born in slavery
601.s: Asked about musical parents, Martin names an uncle, Amos Martin, who played bass horn and drowned before Martin was born. He does not know what band Amos played in.
601.q: I had an uncle, Amos, he played music. That was before I was born. Yes. What instrument did he play? He played bass horn. Bass. Amos Martin.

968.t: Mother's guitar playing and family string sessions
968.s: His mother sang and played guitar well; the family played string instruments together at home, starting with Under the Double Eagle.
968.q: My mother gave me a lot of chords on guitars. Oh, really? Yeah, she really was a good guitar player. Yeah, she really was a good guitar player. Mm-hmm. The fact about it, Bill, we all used to get in the kitchen or the bedroom, my two brothers, my father and my mother, and get to get all string…

475.t: Father's training with Dave Perkins and his age and family order
475.s: His father learned from Dave Perkins, started on tuba, was the oldest brother; Russell asks about bands he played in, including Tuxedo and Eureka.
475.q: played in? Well, my father, most of the band he played, he played with the brass band. And he learned from old man Perkins. Old man Perkins was his teacher.

10.t: Parents, sisters and music at home
10.s: He names his parents, describes his father's fiddle, family quadrilles, coon songs and vaudeville shows at Ramona.
10.ch: Early life and New Orleans arrival
10.q: My father's name was Robert Carew. He ran a shoe store there, a small shoe store there in the neighborhood where we lived in Grand Rapids. My mother's name was Rose, now, I'm getting twisted now, Carolyn, Carolyn, Carolyn Rose, uh, Rosely, Carolyn Rosely Johnson. Her name, her maiden name was. Her…

176.t: Billie's seven sisters and who read music
176.s: She names her sisters, praises Mabel and Sadie at piano, and says she herself plays by ear and does not read.
176.q: Yeah, Mabel was a great piano player. Mabel was a great piano player. And then, the next great piano player was Sadie. So Sadie, she living in Detroit, Michigan now. But she don't care for it much no more.

896.s: His father Charlie played B-flat trumpet in a 15-piece brass band and in small dance bands in the hometown of Colonna; New Orleans musicians sometimes came to play there.
896.q: That's all right. That's all right. I remember my father was in a brass band. He played the brass band. What was his instrument? His instrument was a B-flat trumpet.

312.s: His parents and brother were musical; the family sang four-part harmony and he learned uke and guitar.
312.q: Yes. My father played the banjo and the piano in college and wrote, actually wrote the first Tau Kappa Epsilon sweetheart song. All the fraternities had sweetheart songs. And so he wrote that and played ukulele too I guess. And then my mother sang alto in church choirs and gave piano lessons and…

212.t: Pennywhistle, and no musicians in the family
212.s: The pennywhistle is his only portable instrument. No musical family, though his father organized the church choir parts.
212.q: Yeah. Well it’s the only thing I play that’s portable. You know you really do sometimes just want to play something and you don’t have your tuba in your pocket. The pennywhistle is just the thing.

351.t: The Napoleon brothers and Uncle Phil as a child trumpeter
351.s: Marty's father and uncles were all musicians, and he tells how young Phil found his father's trumpet.
351.q: See the thing, to start it off this way, I usually start off my interviews by saying my father was the oldest of five brothers and one sister. All of the boys were professional musicians. And my father was the oldest, and he played banjo and guitar, my uncle Georgie, George Napoleon played the…

1.t: Mother Rose Barbarin and godfather Paul Barbarin
1.s: His mother was Paul Barbarin's sister, so Paul is his uncle and godfather, who bought his first banjo.
1.ch: Childhood, family and the sounds of New Orleans
1.q: He's my uncle. And he's my godfather. There's this thing that you call like baptizing...you call it... With the Baptists, it's baptism; with the Catholics, it's christening.

89.t: Musical family: parents, circus-clarinet uncle, organ and Scott Joplin
89.s: Both parents were vocal teachers, an uncle played circus clarinet and another uncle played ragtime on the family organ; his younger sister was not musical.
89.q: Yes, yes, yes. I guess it was passed on. My mother was a vocal teacher and a fine singer, and my father was also a vocal teacher. And I had an uncle who played clarinet in the circus and, as I say, my family -- we didn't get a piano until about 1909, but before --

18.t: Anna Mae on music in the family
18.s: She recalls the washboards, tin tubs and an organ, and little J. C. marching in a school concert.
18.ch: Favorite bands, advice and family reflections
18.q: as I can remember. My parents bought an organ. Before then my sisters and brothers, they used to use washboards to make music.

418.t: Pump organ, his father's violin and music at home
418.s: He recalls his grandmother's pump organ, his mother who reportedly played, and his father's beautiful violin playing of reels and Irish tunes.
418.q: Well, there was some organ, the old-time church organ... Before the congregation could afford a pipe organ. It was a pump organ, and people did (?) with their feet. And it's a large thing, with a few scales in it...

413.t: Family music, a cornet at four, siblings and his father's Navy clarinet
413.s: Everyone played by ear in the evenings; his grandfather gave him a cornet at four. He lost a brother in the flu epidemic, and his father was a Navy clarinetist.
413.q: Well, mostly violin, banjos, mandolins, guitars and when I was four my grandfather Maxwell, my father's father, gave me a cor-net. One of my uncles played cor-net and one played baritone horn. But they played mostly old Scotch-Irish songs or they played country music. My grandfather played country…
